When a remote service returns `429 Too Many Requests`, honor `Retry-After` when
the selected retry policy supports it. The outbound client's retry behavior and
the inbound response your own API returns are separate decisions.

Prefer the server's retry guidance when the client policy supports it, instead
of an independent aggressive schedule against a rate-limited dependency.

Check-by-reference against `performance.md` § Outbound Calls: retrying every
exception or HTTP status; retrying unsafe writes without idempotency analysis;
retrying client cancellation; circuit breakers without a failure scenario;
fallback values that conceal incorrect business results; hedged writes; generic
retry wrappers around persistence without understanding provider behavior;
stacked handlers with overlapping strategies; unbounded retry/timeout
combinations.

| Scenario | Default consideration |
|---|---|
| External I/O | Bound execution time |
| Safe transient HTTP failure | Consider retry |
| Unsafe write | No retry unless duplicate-safe |
| `429` from dependency | Respect `Retry-After` where appropriate |
| Repeated dependency outage | Consider circuit breaker |
| Optional data unavailable | Consider explicit fallback |
| Latency-sensitive idempotent read | Consider hedging after measurement |
| Persistence transient faults | Prefer the provider's execution strategy |
| Incoming request rate limiting | ASP.NET Core rate limiter |

canonical_policy.name: C# file and async naming conventions remain conventional
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: For new C# code, prefer file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the project, normally keep one primary top-level type per matching file, and use the Async suffix for Task/ValueTask-returning methods unless an existing or framework contract makes that inappropriate.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Project-consistent file-scoped preference and concrete suggestion0065 match; matching primary-type file default0146 explicitly retains small private/nested locality exception; Async suffix0148 contract-breaking exception already registered.

context_quotes:
For new C# code:

- prefer file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the project;
- by default keep one primary top-level type per file, with the file name
  matching the primary type; small private or nested supporting types may stay
  with the owning type when that improves locality.

Methods returning `Task` or `ValueTask` use the `Async` suffix by default,
following standard .NET conventions and existing interface contracts. Do not
rename framework implementations or established APIs solely to add the suffix
when that would break an existing contract.

Use a regular constructor when validation or initialization is non-trivial,
explicit fields improve readability, the existing codebase consistently uses
that style, or parameter capture would make the class harder to understand. Do
not convert constructors mechanically.

## Records and Classes

Use records when value semantics and immutability are desirable, for example
many DTOs and genuine Value Objects. Use classes when identity, mutable
lifecycle, inheritance, or framework behavior makes class semantics clearer. Do
not turn every DTO or Domain type into a record automatically.

## Visibility and Inheritance

Keep implementation details non-public when they are not part of the project's
public API. Use `sealed` when a type is deliberately not intended for
inheritance and the modifier communicates useful design intent; do not add
`sealed` merely as a speculative JIT optimization.

## Modern Syntax and Type Inference

Use collection expressions, pattern matching, switch expressions,
target-typed construction, and other modern features when they make the code
easier to read; do not prefer newer syntax when the result is less obvious. Use
`var` when the type is obvious from the right-hand side or not important to
understanding the code; use an explicit type when it improves clarity.

## Naming

Use standard .NET naming: PascalCase for types, methods, properties, and public
members; camelCase for parameters and local variables; meaningful names over
abbreviations. Private-field naming follows the repository's established
convention.
